Part A · Chapter A5

Decision trees

Grow a tree one question at a time, and see that more questions can raise training accuracy without raising held-out accuracy.

A decision tree sorts examples into boxes with yes/no questions about measurements. This chapter reads a tree, scores a question by Gini impurity, grows a tree by greedy search on the made-up SharkCam catch table, shows how a deep tree can fit the quirks of its training sharks, and ends with trees that predict a number.

Trees are the building blocks of the boosted models of the next chapter.

You will need: recursion and trees from the toolkit, the idea of a model and a baseline, and the idea of a held-out set from A4. A short reminder appears where the held-out set is used.

The data. The sharks here come from the made-up SharkCam catch table: 600 records generated from published length-weight relationships, not field data. Sharks whose tag number ends in 0, 1 or 2 (164 sharks) are held out and never used to grow a tree. The other 436 sharks, 196 of them spadenose, are the training sharks.

Reading a tree

Guess first. A shark is 41 cm long and was found at 18 m. Is it a spadenose shark? If you could ask one question about the shark first, would you ask about its length or its depth?

A decision tree is a chain of yes/no questions in which the answer to one question picks the next. Here a question compares one measurement of a shark (its length or its depth) with a threshold, as in “length at most 50.35 cm?”. The answers for one shark form a path that ends in a box, a rectangle of the plot. The call of a box is the more common label (spadenose or other shark) among the training sharks in it, the 436 sharks the tree is built from. Because the call belongs to the box, all sharks that end in it get the same call. The training accuracy of a tree is the share of training sharks whose call is right. The other 164 sharks are held out, kept for testing.

  1. Coral diamonds are spadenose sharks and navy dots are other sharks. The ring starts on Tag 3305 (41.0 cm, found at 18 m), and the highlighted path in the tree leads to box 2.
  2. Press Tag 4127 and then Tag 5519, and the ring moves to box 1 and then to box 4, with the call shown under the figure. Drag the ring across the plot, and the path changes only where the ring crosses an edge between boxes.

A 41 cm shark found at 18 m (Tag 3305) ends in box 2, where 179 of the 201 training sharks are spadenose, so the call is spadenose.

How it works

Take Tag 3305, 41.0 cm long and found at 18 m. The tree asks “length at most 50.35 cm?”. If the answer is yes, the next question is “depth at most 5.65 m?”, which leads to box 1 (yes) or box 2 (no). If the answer is no, the next question is “length at most 59.85 cm?”, which leads to box 3 (yes) or box 4 (no). For Tag 3305 the answers are yes and then no, so it ends in box 2. That box has 201 training sharks, 179 of them spadenose (179 ÷ 201 = 89%), so the call is spadenose.

A box's call is right for the training sharks in it whose label is the call, so the four boxes give the training accuracy:

(17box 1: all other sharks+179box 2: spadenose, of 201+40box 3: other sharks, of 57+161box 4: all other sharks)÷436training sharks=91.1%training accuracy

Common belief. The 89% of box 2 is the chance that a new shark in box 2 is a spadenose.

Why it fails. It is the share of the training sharks, so it describes those sharks and not new ones. Of the 71 held-out sharks in box 2, 60 are spadenose, about 85%.

Better account. Read the 89% as a summary of the training sharks, and test on held-out sharks, because the tree never used them.

Quick quiz

A 70 cm shark was found at 3 m. Which box does it end in, and what is its call?

Box 4. The answers are no to “length ≤ 50.35 cm?” and no to “length ≤ 59.85 cm?”. The depth question is never asked, because the path never reaches it. The call is other shark, because box 4 has 161 training sharks, none of them spadenose.

Why does box 2 call all its sharks spadenose when 22 of its 201 training sharks are other sharks?

The call is the more common label. A box gives one answer to all sharks in it, so the sharks of the other label in that box are called wrongly.

Terms

split
one question about one measurement, such as "length at most 50.35 cm?"
leaf (box)
where a path of questions ends; on the plot it is a rectangle
depth

The other two tags

The tree was grown on the 436 training sharks and is only two questions deep, so its depth is 2. Coral diamonds are spadenose sharks and navy dots are other sharks (milk, bamboo, hammerhead and Ganges). The ring starts on Tag 3305, the Sassoon spadenose from the made-up table.

Now press Tag 4127, the juvenile bamboo shark from the Juhu rock pool. Its length is also under 50.35 cm, but it was found at 0.4 m, so it falls in box 1, which has no spadenose at all. Tag 5519, the young hammerhead, is longer than 59.85 cm and ends in box 4. The shallow-water question works in this table because the made-up dives in rock pools are shallow and mostly record bamboo sharks (of the 21 training sharks found at 5.65 m or less, 17 are bamboo sharks and 4 are hammerheads). A tree learns whatever pattern the table has, including quirks of how the table was made.

A second case

A second case, a shark that is not one of the three. A shark of 55 cm found at 2 m answers "no" to "length ≤ 50.35 cm?" and "yes" to "length ≤ 59.85 cm?". It ends in box 3, which has 57 training sharks, 17 of them spadenose. The call is "other shark", which is right for 40 of the 57, or 70%. This is the weakest box. The 17 spadenose sharks in it are all called wrongly.

Trees are recursive

A tree is a recursive object, as in the toolkit chapter on recursion. Below the first question hangs a smaller tree for the sharks that said yes, and another for the sharks that said no. Predicting walks down one path, and the number of questions asked is at most the depth.

Two details of the boxes

Two details help when you read a tree. The threshold 50.35 lies halfway between the neighbouring training lengths 50.3 and 50.4, so no training shark lies on the line. And all the edges of the boxes are parallel to an axis. A rule that slants, such as "heavier than expected for its length", needs a staircase of small boxes to approximate it.

Twenty questions

A tree resembles the game of twenty questions. The answers narrow the set of animals one by one, and the last answer names one. In the game a person invents a new question while thinking about the animal. A tree may only ask “is this measurement at most some threshold?”, and all its questions were fixed during training. The 89% of box 2 is also only the share of training sharks in the box, and nobody has tested it as a chance for a new shark (A4).

In practice

In practice, read a tree from its leaves first. Print the number of training sharks and the class counts in the leaves, and look for leaves with few sharks. The code below does this for the tree of the figure, written out as nested questions.

Debug tip. Check how many training sharks are in the box that makes a call. A box with 3 sharks that "shows 100% spadenose" says much less than a box with 160 sharks at 89%.

In Python

import numpy as np, pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("catch.csv")                  # made-up records
train = df[df.record_id % 10 >= 3]             # tags ending 0, 1, 2 are held out
L, d = train.length_cm.to_numpy(), train.depth_m.to_numpy()
spade = (train.species == "spadenose").to_numpy()

def box(length, depth):                        # the tree of the figure
    if length <= 50.35:
        return 1 if depth <= 5.65 else 2
    return 3 if length <= 59.85 else 4

boxes = np.array([box(a, b) for a, b in zip(L, d)])
right = 0
for b in (1, 2, 3, 4):
    n, k = (boxes == b).sum(), spade[boxes == b].sum()
    call = "spadenose" if k > n - k else "other"
    right += max(k, n - k)
    print(f"box {b}: {n:3d} sharks, {k:3d} spadenose, call {call}")
print("training accuracy", round(right / len(L), 3))

for tag, length, depth in [(3305, 41.0, 18.0), (4127, 44.0, 0.4), (5519, 82.0, 14.0)]:
    print("Tag", tag, "-> box", box(length, depth))
box 1:  17 sharks,   0 spadenose, call other
box 2: 201 sharks, 179 spadenose, call spadenose
box 3:  57 sharks,  17 spadenose, call other
box 4: 161 sharks,   0 spadenose, call other
training accuracy 0.911
Tag 3305 -> box 2
Tag 4127 -> box 1
Tag 5519 -> box 4

The four boxes match the figure, and the accuracy 0.911 matches the sum above. Tags 3305, 4127 and 5519 end in boxes 2, 1 and 4, as in the figure.

More questions

Box 1 has 17 training sharks and none is a spadenose. Does that show that a new shark in box 1 is certainly not a spadenose?

No. If 10% of all sharks in that region were spadenose, the chance of 0 in 17 is \(0.9^{17} = 0.17\), about 1 in 6. A box of 17 sharks cannot rule out a share of 10%.

Scoring a question: Gini impurity

Guess first. Box A has 10 spadenose and 10 other sharks. Box B has 18 spadenose and 2 other sharks. Which box is "more mixed", and would you say it is twice as mixed or more?

A good question leaves two boxes that, taken together, are purer than the box it started from. The Gini impurity \(G\) of a box measures how mixed it is. \(G\) is the chance that two sharks drawn at random from the box (the first put back before the second draw) have different labels (spadenose or other shark). If \(p_0\) and \(p_1\) are the shares of the two labels, the two draws match with probability \(p_0^2 + p_1^2\). So \(G = 1 - p_0^2 - p_1^2\), which is 0 for a box with one label and 0.5 for an even mix. A split is a question that divides a box into a yes side and a no side. The weighted Gini after a split is the \(G\) of the two sides averaged with weights equal to their numbers of sharks. The drop is \(G\) before the split minus this weighted Gini. A split never raises the weighted Gini, and the fold gives the reason.

  1. Coral diamonds are spadenose sharks and navy dots are other sharks, here 24 training sharks placed by length. The divider starts with 12 sharks on the yes side, and the weighted Gini (“G after” in the equation rows) is 0.215, against 0.497 for the whole row (“G before”).
  2. Drag the divider to put 9 sharks on the yes side. That side now has only spadenose sharks, and the weighted Gini falls to 0.144.
  3. On the curve, the black dot is the whole row, the two coloured dots are its sides, and the weighted Gini is the point on the dashed line under the black dot.

The weighted Gini is lowest, at 0.144, when the yes side is the 9 shortest sharks, all spadenose.

How it works

Take the boxes of the guess. Box A (shares 0.5 and 0.5) has \(G = 1 - 0.25 - 0.25 = 0.50\), and box B (shares 0.1 and 0.9) has \(G = 1 - 0.01 - 0.81 = 0.18\). Box A's \(G\) is 0.50 ÷ 0.18 = 2.8 times box B's, so by this measure the answer to the guess is more than twice.

Now take the first question of the tree, “length at most 50.35 cm?”. Before it, the 436 training sharks (240 other, 196 spadenose) have \(G = 1 - (240/436)^2 - (196/436)^2 = 1 - 0.303 - 0.202 = 0.495\). Both sides have 218 sharks, so the weighted Gini after the question is the average of their \(G\) values, and the drop is 0.495 minus that average:

0.5yes side, 218 of 436×0.294G, yes side (39 other, 179 spadenose)+0.5no side, 218 of 436×0.144G, no side (201 other, 17 spadenose)=0.219G after⇒0.276drop

Common belief. The best question is the one that gets the most sharks right.

Why it fails. In box 2 of the tree of the previous section (22 other, 179 spadenose), “length at most 42.65 cm?” sends 4 other and 130 spadenose sharks to the yes side. The no side gets 18 other and 49 spadenose sharks. Both sides call spadenose, so the right calls stay at 179, yet the weighted Gini falls from 0.195 to 0.170, because the yes side is almost pure.

Better account. A split that changes no call can still lower the weighted Gini, which shows progress that the count of right calls cannot.

Quick quiz

What is \(G\) for a box with 5 spadenose and 5 other sharks, and for one with only spadenose?

For 5 and 5: \(1 - 0.5^2 - 0.5^2 = 0.5\). For a box with one label: \(1 - 1^2 - 0^2 = 0\).

A box has 49 other sharks and 1 spadenose. What is \(G\), and what does it say?

\(G = 1 - 0.98^2 - 0.02^2 = 0.039\). The box is almost pure, so one more question gains little there.

Go deeper reading the curve, formula, entropy, Python about 3 min

Reading the figure

The row shows 24 training sharks under 100 cm, drawn at random and placed by length. Drag the divider, or move the slider, and read the equation boxes. On the right, the curve shows \(G\) for any possible share of spadenose in a box. It is 0 for a box with only one class and reaches 0.5 for an even mix. The black dot is the box before the split, and the two coloured dots are the two sides after it.

The dashed line joins the two sides. The weighted Gini after the split is the point on that line directly under the black dot, because the weights are the sizes of the sides. The coral bar is the drop. The curve bends downward, so that point can never lie above the curve. A split therefore never raises the weighted Gini. It lowers it unless both sides have the same share as the box did.

The formulas

\[ G = 1 - \sum_{k} p_k^{2}, \qquad G_{\text{after}} = \frac{n_L}{n}\,G_L + \frac{n_R}{n}\,G_R, \qquad \text{drop} = G_{\text{before}} - G_{\text{after}} \]

  • \(p_k\) is the share of class \(k\) (label \(k\)) in the box. With two classes, \(G = 1 - p_0^2 - p_1^2 = 2p_1(1-p_1)\).
  • \(n\) is the number of sharks in the box. \(n_L\) and \(n_R\) are the numbers that answer yes (left) and no (right).
  • \(G_L\) and \(G_R\) are the impurities of the yes side and the no side, found with the same formula.

How the scale bends

The scale bends with the shares. A minority share of 10% already gives 0.18, and a share of 2% (49 against 1) gives 0.04.

Size matters: a second split

A second split of the training sharks shows how size matters. The question "depth ≤ 5.65 m?" sends 21 sharks to the yes side, all of them other sharks, so \(G = 0\). The other 415 sharks answer no. They are 219 other and 196 spadenose, so \(G = 0.4985\). The weighted Gini is \(21/436 \times 0 + 415/436 \times 0.4985 = 0.4745\), and the drop from 0.495 is about 0.02. A pure side helps little when it is small, and 21 sharks are 5% of the box.

In practice

In practice, Gini is the default score of scikit-learn. Entropy, \(-\sum_k p_k \log_2 p_k\), is the other common score. For two classes it rises and falls like the Gini curve, and the two usually choose the same split. Be careful with a measurement that has many distinct values. It offers many cut points, so the best of them can look good by luck. A large Gini drop is a reason to test the tree on held-out sharks, and not a result in itself.

Debug tip. If a split gives a drop of 0 or close to it, check the threshold. A cut at the very edge of the range sends nearly all sharks to one side, so the weighted Gini stays at its old value.

Used in: Gini impurity is the score the greedy search lowers in the next section. Boosted trees in A6 use a different score, built from the leftover errors, but the splitting search is the same.

In Python

import numpy as np

def gini(counts):
    p = np.array(counts) / sum(counts)
    return 1 - np.sum(p ** 2)

print(round(gini([10, 10]), 3), round(gini([18, 2]), 3), gini([20, 0]))

# the first question on the 436 training sharks: counts are [other, spadenose]
before = gini([240, 196])
yes, no = [39, 179], [201, 17]
after = (218 * gini(yes) + 218 * gini(no)) / 436
print(round(before, 3), round(after, 4), round(before - after, 3))
0.5 0.18 0.0
0.495 0.2188 0.276

More questions

Why is the weighted Gini after a split never above the Gini before it?

The Gini curve bends downward. The weighted average of the two sides is a point on the straight line between them, and that line stays on or below the curve at the box's own share.

Growing a tree: the greedy search

Guess first. To find the best question about length for the 436 training sharks, the computer tries thresholds between neighbouring lengths. About how many thresholds: 5, 50, 300 or 4,000? And would you cut length first, or depth?

A tree is grown greedily, which means choosing the best question for the box in front of you without looking ahead. For one box, the computer scans the thresholds of both measurements (the numbers in questions such as “length at most 50.35 cm?”). All thresholds between the same two neighbouring values give the same two groups, so the scan tries one threshold halfway between neighbours. It scores them one after another by the weighted Gini they leave (the \(G\) of the two new boxes, averaged with weights equal to their numbers of sharks) and keeps the lowest. Then it repeats this inside the two new boxes. The fold explains why the scan is fast, gives the code (best_split) and names the base cases of the repetition.

  1. With Ask about set to length, drag the line on the plot or the Threshold slider, and read the weighted Gini (“G after”) in the equation rows. The small chart “Impurity after the split, by length threshold” scores all thresholds, so its lowest point is the best length question.
  2. Press “Let the computer choose”. It scans the thresholds of length and then of depth, and stops at the lowest point of either chart: length ≤ 50.35 cm, with weighted Gini 0.219.
  3. Press “Split here”, click a box to choose the next one, and split again. The last readout, “Computer's best”, shows the weighted Gini of the greedy tree with the same number of boxes as yours. For four boxes it is 0.145, and a tree of your own can score lower.

The scan tries 304 thresholds of length and scores lowest at 50.35 cm, with weighted Gini 0.219, while the best depth threshold, 5.65 m, scores 0.4745.

How it works

Scan the lengths of the training sharks. These 436 sharks have 305 different lengths, so the scan tries 304 thresholds, which answers the guess (about 300). The lowest weighted Gini, 0.219, comes at 50.35 cm. For depth the lowest is 0.4745 at 5.65 m, which puts 21 sharks, all other sharks, on the yes side:

21/436yes side: 21 sharks×0G, all other sharks+415/436no side: 415 sharks×0.4985G, 219 other, 196 spadenose=0.4745weighted Gini

Here the pure side is small: the 21 sharks are 5% of the 436, and the 415 on the no side are as mixed as the whole box (0.4985, against 0.495), so the weighted Gini falls only a little. By comparison, both sides of the length question are purer than the whole box.

Common belief. The computer finds the best possible tree.

Why it fails. Greedy search never looks ahead, so it can miss questions that work only together. Take four points where (0, 0) and (1, 1) have one label and (0, 1) and (1, 0) have the other. Any first question leaves both sides as mixed as the whole, so the weighted Gini stays at 0.5. A search that stops when the drop is 0 would stop here, yet two questions in a row separate the points perfectly.

Better account. Greedy search is fast and often good, but a better tree may exist. Check the tree on held-out sharks.

Quick quiz

Why does a tree scan thresholds only between neighbouring different values?

Any threshold between the same two neighbouring values gives the same two groups, so trying one of them is enough. A cut between two equal values cannot separate them at all.

The question “depth at most 5.65 m?” makes a pure yes side of 21 sharks, yet scores 0.4745. Why is it far above 0.219?

The pure side is small. The 21 sharks are 5% of the 436, and the other 415 are as mixed as the whole box, so the weighted Gini falls only from 0.495 to 0.4745.

Terms

cut, cut point
other names for a threshold, seen as a position in the sorted row of values
depth limit
a cap on the number of questions in a row, set so that a tree stops growing

Using the figure

Start with one box that has all 436 training sharks. Choose a measurement, drag the line, and read the three rows of boxes under the plot. When you like the line, press "Split here". Click any box, on the plot or in the tree, to pick the next one to split. The small charts score all thresholds in the chosen box. Their lowest point is the best question for that measurement.

Now press "Let the computer choose". It sweeps through the thresholds of length, then of depth, and draws their scores. At the end it moves to the lowest point of either chart. For the first box, that is "length ≤ 50.35 cm". Try this exercise: can you beat the computer's total score for four boxes, shown at the bottom of the figure? Greedy search is not guaranteed to find the lowest total score, and here it misses a lower one for four boxes. Ask “depth ≤ 5.65 m?” first, then “length ≤ 47.2 cm?” among the 415 sharks found deeper, and then “length ≤ 55.5 cm?” among those longer than 47.2 cm. The weighted Gini is 0.140, against the computer's 0.145, although the tree is right for fewer training sharks (390 against 397).

Why the scan is fast

How does the computer try 300 thresholds so fast? It sorts the lengths once. A cut between neighbouring lengths is a position in the sorted row, and moving the cut one place to the right changes only one shark's side. So the counts on both sides update with a running total, and a threshold costs one small calculation. The total work for one measurement is about the cost of the sort, \(n \log n\) steps (toolkit chapter on Big-O). Cuts between equal lengths are skipped, because no question can separate two sharks of the same length. The 436 training sharks have 305 different lengths, so there are 304 cut points.

\[ (j^{*}, t^{*}) = \arg\min_{j,\,t}\; \Big(\tfrac{n_L}{n}\,G_L + \tfrac{n_R}{n}\,G_R\Big) \]

  • \(j\) is the measurement to ask about (length or depth) and \(t\) the threshold.
  • \(j^{*}, t^{*}\) are the winning choices: the pair with the lowest weighted Gini over all measurements and all thresholds.
  • The terms inside the bracket are the weighted impurity of the yes side and the no side, as in the last section.

The scan in NumPy

Here is the scan in NumPy, on ten made-up sharks. The function sorts the lengths, keeps running counts of spadenose on the yes side, and scores all cuts at once.

import numpy as np

def gini(n0, n1):
    n = n0 + n1
    return 1 - (n0 / n) ** 2 - (n1 / n) ** 2

def best_split(x, y):
    order = np.argsort(x)
    x, y = x[order], y[order]
    n = len(y)
    n1_left = np.cumsum(y)[:-1]             # spadenose among the first i sharks
    n_left = np.arange(1, n)                # size of the yes side for each cut
    n1_right = y.sum() - n1_left
    n_right = n - n_left
    g_left = 1 - (n1_left / n_left) ** 2 - (1 - n1_left / n_left) ** 2
    g_right = 1 - (n1_right / n_right) ** 2 - (1 - n1_right / n_right) ** 2
    score = (n_left * g_left + n_right * g_right) / n
    score[x[1:] == x[:-1]] = np.inf         # no cut between equal values
    i = score.argmin()
    return (x[i] + x[i + 1]) / 2, score[i]

# ten sharks, made up for this example
length = np.array([36.0, 41.0, 44.4, 47.2, 52.0, 55.3, 61.8, 64.3, 70.1, 82.0])
spade  = np.array([1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0])
t, s = best_split(length, spade)
print(round(float(t), 2), round(float(s), 3))
print(round(gini(5, 5), 3))
49.6 0.167
0.5

The best cut is at 49.6 cm. It puts four spadenose on the yes side, and the one spadenose in the other six sharks leaves the no side mixed. The weighted Gini drops from 0.5 to 0.167.

Check the 0.167 by hand. The yes side has 4 sharks, all spadenose, so \(G = 0\). The no side has 6 sharks, 1 spadenose and 5 other, so \(G = 1 - (1/6)^2 - (5/6)^2 = 0.278\). The weighted Gini is \(0.4 \times 0 + 0.6 \times 0.278 = 0.167\). A worse cut, at 38.5 cm, puts one spadenose alone on the yes side. The no side then has 9 sharks, 4 of them spadenose, with \(G = 0.494\). The weighted Gini is \(0.9 \times 0.494 = 0.444\), nearly as bad as no split at all.

The scan has a tie. A cut at 58.55 cm also scores 0.167: the yes side has 6 sharks with 5 spadenose, and the no side is pure. The code returns the first of equal scores, which is 49.6 cm. Larger tables have ties too, so the tree you get can depend on the order of the rows or on the random seed of the library. Two trees with the same score are equally good on the training sharks and can differ on new ones.

The same function on the training table

Now the same function on the training table:

import pandas as pd                                   # best_split and gini come from the block above
df = pd.read_csv("catch.csv")                         # made-up records
train = df[df.record_id % 10 >= 3]                    # tags ending in 0, 1, 2 are held out
y = (train.species == "spadenose").to_numpy().astype(int)
print(len(y), y.sum(), round(gini(len(y) - y.sum(), y.sum()), 3))
for col in ["length_cm", "depth_m"]:
    t, s = best_split(train[col].to_numpy(), y)
    print(col, round(float(t), 2), round(float(s), 4))
436 196 0.495
length_cm 50.35 0.2188
depth_m 5.65 0.4745

Length wins with 0.2188 against 0.4745, as in the figure. After the first split, the same search is run again in both new boxes, and again in their children. That is recursion (0.2): the base case is a box that is pure, too small, or at the depth limit.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. A split that scores well because one side has a single shark is a trap. A box of one shark is always pure, and it says little about the next shark. Set a smallest box size, as in the next section, before trusting a deep tree.

The same tree in scikit-learn

import pandas as pd
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, export_text
df = pd.read_csv("catch.csv")
df["spadenose"] = (df.species == "spadenose").astype(int)
held = df.record_id % 10 < 3
X = ["length_cm", "depth_m"]
tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=2, random_state=0).fit(df[~held][X], df[~held].spadenose)
print(export_text(tree, feature_names=X))
print("train", round(tree.score(df[~held][X], df[~held].spadenose), 4), "held-out", round(tree.score(df[held][X], df[held].spadenose), 4))
|--- length_cm <= 50.35
|   |--- depth_m <= 5.65
|   |   |--- class: 0
|   |--- depth_m >  5.65
|   |   |--- class: 1
|--- length_cm >  50.35
|   |--- length_cm <= 59.85
|   |   |--- class: 0
|   |--- length_cm >  59.85
|   |   |--- class: 0

train 0.9106 held-out 0.8598

This is the tree from the first figure, with a training accuracy of 91.1% and a held-out accuracy of 86.0%. Class 1 is spadenose.

In practice

In practice, two limits do most of the work: max_depth (3 to 8 is a common range) and min_samples_leaf (5 to 20 for a few hundred rows). Choose them with cross-validation on the training sharks (A4). A depth-limited tree is also a useful baseline for the models of the next chapter.

Where this is used

Bridge to my project. My diabetes screening project used the same tree idea on the Pima data: 768 women of Pima heritage, measured in the United States, so not data from Mumbai. Its primer splits glucose and BMI into four boxes. The final model in my report was XGBoost, a library for boosted trees (A6).

The XOR example

The four points of the break are the pattern XOR from the logic section, where two measurements matter only together.

More questions

The first split gives a weighted Gini of 0.219 and splitting the more mixed box next gives 0.162. What did the second split improve, and is the search done?

It lowered the weighted Gini of the whole tree by further splitting one box. The search is done only when the depth limit, the smallest box size, or purity stops it. A box that is already pure needs no more questions.

On the ten sharks, a cut at 38.5 cm puts 1 spadenose on the yes side and 9 sharks (4 spadenose, 5 other) on the no side. What is the weighted Gini?

The yes side is pure, so \(G = 0\). The no side has \(G = 1 - (4/9)^2 - (5/9)^2 = 0.494\). The weighted Gini is \(0.9 \times 0.494 = 0.444\), far above the best cut's 0.167.

Depth, memorising and held-out accuracy

Guess first. You let the tree ask 12 questions in a row instead of 2. Will it do better on sharks it has never seen? What do you expect its accuracy to be on the sharks it trained on?

The depth of a tree (not the depth in metres where a shark was found) is the largest number of questions asked in a row on one path, and a depth limit stops the tree from growing deeper. In this example a deeper tree has more boxes and fits the training sharks better, but its held-out accuracy does not rise with it. Held-out accuracy is the share of right calls among the 164 sharks kept out of the growing. This is overfitting: training accuracy climbs while held-out accuracy does not. This may be because the extra boxes fit quirks of the training sharks, which new sharks do not share. The fold also explains why a tree needs no rescaling of lengths or depths.

  1. The navy curve is the training accuracy and the coral curve is the held-out accuracy. At the starting depth limit of 2 the tree has 4 boxes, with 91.1% right on the training sharks and 86.0% on the held-out sharks.
  2. Press Play, or drag Depth limit, to deepen the tree one level at a time. At depth 12 the training curve is at 99.5%, while the held-out curve stays between 83.5% and 86.0% from depth 2 on.
  3. With the depth limit at 12, raise Smallest box allowed, the fewest training sharks a box may have, to 20. The tree shrinks to 10 boxes, the training curve falls back to 90.4%, and the held-out accuracy is 86.0%.

From depth 2 to depth 12 the training accuracy climbs from 91.1% to 99.5%, while the held-out accuracy stays between 83.5% and 86.0%.

How it works

Depth 2 against depth 12. The depth-2 tree has 4 boxes and is right for 397 of the 436 training sharks (91.1%) and 141 of the 164 held-out sharks (86.0%). The depth-12 tree has 50 boxes, so it is right for more training sharks, 434 (99.5%), but for only 139 held-out sharks (84.8%).

46extra boxes: 50 − 4⇒+37training sharks right: 434 − 397and−2held-out sharks right: 139 − 141

The 46 extra boxes add under one right training shark per box, and remove 2 right held-out sharks (1.2 points). On 164 held-out sharks the standard error of an accuracy (how much it varies between held-out sets of that size) is \(\sqrt{0.86 \times 0.14 / 164} = 0.027\), about 2.7 points. So a change of one or two sharks between depths is small next to this noise.

Common belief. A tree with 100% training accuracy is a perfect model.

Why it fails. The depth-12 tree is right for 434 of 436 training sharks and wrong for 25 of the 164 held-out sharks. So near-perfect training accuracy says little about new sharks. Its gap between training and held-out accuracy is 14.8 points, against 5.1 at depth 2.

Better account. Accuracy on held-out sharks estimates how the tree will do on new sharks, and a baseline, a simple answer to compare with, shows whether that number is good. Always answering “other shark” is right for 56% of the held-out sharks (92 of 164).

Quick quiz

The tree has 99.8% training accuracy and 85% held-out accuracy. What is the gap, and what does it suggest?

About 15 points. It suggests overfitting: many small boxes that fit quirks of the training sharks.

Depth 2 gets 141 of 164 held-out sharks right and depth 6 gets 140. Is depth 6 worse?

No clear difference. One shark of 164 is 0.6 points, far inside the noise of about 2.7 points. The depth-6 tree is more complex for no visible gain, so the simpler tree is the better choice.

Terms

held-out accuracy
the share of sharks right among sharks the tree never saw while growing (A4)
overfitting
fitting the quirks of the training sharks, so that training accuracy climbs while held-out accuracy does not (A4)
smallest box
the fewest training sharks a box may have; a larger number stops the tree from making tiny boxes

Reading the curves

With no depth limit the tree grows to 51 leaves for 436 training sharks, so several boxes have only one or two sharks. A box of one shark is right about that shark by construction. The faint coral lines show the held-out accuracy of the same recipe on 20 other random splits of the 600 sharks into training and held-out sets. The dashed line is their average. They rise steeply from depth 0 to 2, from 55.5% to 86.9%, and then drift down slowly, to 84.0% at depth 12. The gap between the training and held-out lines is a sign of overfitting. Here it grows from 5 points at depth 2 to about 15 points at depth 12.

Noise in the held-out accuracy

One held-out set of 164 sharks is also a noisy test. The held-out accuracy at depth 2 is 86.0%, and the sampling noise on that number is about 2.7 points (0.7):

0.027standard error=√(0.86accuracy p×0.141 − p÷164held-out sharks)

So the curves at depth 2, 3, 4 and 5 are the same within noise. Do not read a gap of half a point between two depths as a finding. Choose a depth from the curves, take the simplest tree on the plateau, and test it once on data that played no part in the choice.

No feature scaling

Trees also need no feature scaling. A question compares one measurement with one threshold. If length were written in inches, all thresholds would be divided by 2.54 and no shark would change boxes. This differs from the models of A2, where the scale of a feature changes how fast gradient descent moves.

In practice

In practice, choose the depth and the smallest box with cross-validation on the training sharks (A4), and not on the held-out sharks. For a few hundred rows, try depths 2 to 8 and smallest boxes of 5 to 20. Keep the simplest tree whose score is within the noise of the best. A tree deeper than the data support models the quirks of the training sharks.

Debug tip. When training accuracy is near 100% and held-out accuracy is far lower, cut the depth, raise the smallest box size, or both. Then compare the gap again.

In Python

import pandas as pd
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

df = pd.read_csv("catch.csv")                  # made-up records
df["spadenose"] = (df.species == "spadenose").astype(int)
held = df.record_id % 10 < 3
X = ["length_cm", "depth_m"]
tr, he = df[~held], df[held]

def run(label, seed=0, **kw):
    t = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=seed, **kw).fit(tr[X], tr.spadenose)
    a, b = t.score(tr[X], tr.spadenose), t.score(he[X], he.spadenose)
    print(f"{label:16s} leaves {t.get_n_leaves():2d}  train {a:.1%}  held-out {b:.1%}")

for depth in (1, 2, 3, 6):
    run(f"depth {depth}", max_depth=depth)
run("depth 12", seed=1, max_depth=12)         # seed 1 breaks ties as the figure does
run("no limit")
run("smallest box 20", min_samples_leaf=20)
depth 1          leaves  2  train 87.2%  held-out 82.9%
depth 2          leaves  4  train 91.1%  held-out 86.0%
depth 3          leaves  6  train 91.3%  held-out 85.4%
depth 6          leaves 24  train 94.0%  held-out 85.4%
depth 12         leaves 50  train 99.5%  held-out 84.8%
no limit         leaves 51  train 99.8%  held-out 83.5%
smallest box 20  leaves 10  train 90.4%  held-out 86.0%

The first five rows match the figure. When two cuts score the same, scikit-learn picks between them with its random seed, and only deep trees have enough ties to notice. Over seeds 0 to 99, the depth-12 tree gets between 135 and 140 of the 164 held-out sharks right. Seed 1 gives the figure's 139. Without a depth limit the tree grows one more level, to 51 leaves.

More questions

Why are depth 3 and depth 5 hard to tell apart in the figure?

Their held-out accuracies differ by less than the noise of a 164-shark held-out set, which is about 2.7 points.

Trees that predict a number

Guess first. A tree predicts a spadenose shark's weight from its length. Sketch what its graph looks like: is it a line, a curve, or something else?

A regression tree is a tree whose boxes answer with a number instead of a label. A box is scored by its squared error, the sum over its training sharks of (weight − the box's average weight)2. It answers with that average, the single number with the smallest squared error for those weights. The graph of the answers against length is a step function: flat in pieces called steps, one per box, with jumps between them, because a box gives one answer for all lengths in it. A tree's error on a set of sharks is its RMSE, the root mean squared error. Here the miss of a shark is the gap between the tree's answer and its recorded weight, and the RMSE is the square root of the average squared miss.

  1. The navy dots are the training spadenose sharks and the teal staircase is the tree's answer at depth 3, with 8 steps. Lower Depth limit to 0, and the staircase is one step at the average weight, 0.219 kg, with a training error of 0.134 kg. Raise it to 3, and the training error falls to 0.036 kg.
  2. Drag “Ask the tree about length” to 41 cm. The tree says 0.215 kg, and the equation row shows how: 4.509 ÷ 21 = 0.215 kg, the average weight of the 21 training sharks in that step.
  3. Drag it on to 70 cm and switch on “the rule behind the data”, the length-weight law that generated these made-up weights. The tree says 0.700 kg, the height of its last step, where the rule says 1.088 kg.

At depth 3 the tree's held-out error is 0.045 kg, against 0.158 kg for the average and 0.048 kg for a straight line, but it stays flat beyond 59.8 cm.

How it works

Take Tag 3305 (41.0 cm, 0.228 kg recorded). At depth 3 the tree puts it in the step for lengths from 39.45 to 42.15 cm, a step with 21 training sharks. Their weights add up to 4.509 kg, so the tree answers 4.509 ÷ 21 = 0.215 kg and misses by 0.228 − 0.215 = 0.013 kg.

The search is as before, but a question is scored by the squared errors of its two new boxes, added together. For the first question, “length at most 42.15 cm?”, the whole box of 196 training sharks divides into two boxes. The whole box has average 0.219 kg and squared error 3.544 kg2, and the two new boxes add up to 1.292 kg2:

3.544squared error, whole box: 196 sharks−0.435yes side: 126 sharks−0.857no side: 70 sharks=2.252drop in squared error

Analogy. A regression tree is a staircase laid against a smooth hill. The steps are the averages of the boxes, the hill is the rule behind the data, and more steps follow the training weights more closely.

Where it breaks. A staircase has a last step, so beyond the longest training shark the tree stays flat. At 70 cm the tree answers 0.700 kg, as it does at 60 cm, while the rule gives 1.088 kg there. More steps also stop helping on new sharks: here the held-out error is lowest at depth 4, 0.041 kg, and rises after it.

Quick quiz

What does a box of a regression tree answer, and why that number?

The average of the training values in the box, because the average is the single number with the smallest squared error for those values.

A box has three sharks that weigh 0.50, 0.55 and 0.60 kg. What does it answer, and what is its squared error?

It answers the average, 0.55 kg, so the squared error is \((-0.05)^2 + 0^2 + 0.05^2 = 0.005\). Any other answer gives a larger sum.

Go deeper the right box, why the average, Python, boosting about 5 min

Terms

squared error
the squared gap between a prediction and the true value, as in A2

The data and the numbers

The figure uses the 196 spadenose sharks in the training sharks and 72 held-out spadenose sharks. The two rows of boxes below the plot show the average of the step under the ask line and the squared errors of the first question.

At depth 3 the tree has an error (RMSE) of 0.036 kg on its training sharks and 0.045 kg on held-out sharks. Always answering with the average weight gives 0.134 kg and 0.158 kg, and a straight line (A2) gives 0.047 kg and 0.048 kg. Deeper trees keep lowering the training error and stop helping the held-out error after depth 4, the same pattern as in the last section.

Beyond the data

The made-up table has no spadenose shark above 60 cm, so the tree repeats the last step, about 0.70 kg. The rule that made the data, \(W = 0.0044\,L^{2.923}\) grams, gives about 1.1 kg at 70 cm. A tree cannot extend a trend beyond its data. A straight line fitted to the training sharks keeps rising, but it gives only 0.688 kg at 70 cm.

The formulas

\[ \text{leaf value} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i\,\in\,\text{box}} y_i, \qquad \text{error of a box} = \sum_{i\,\in\,\text{box}} \big(y_i - \text{leaf value}\big)^{2} \]

  • \(y_i\) is the weight of training shark \(i\), and \(n\) the number of training sharks in the box.
  • The leaf value is the average of those weights. The best single number for a box under squared error is its average.
  • The search picks the question that makes the error of the two new boxes, added together, as small as possible.

The next question, and the right box

The two averages that the first question leaves, 0.139 kg and 0.363 kg, are the answers of its two boxes. Subtract the overall average 0.219 and you get −0.080 and +0.144, the first stump of A6. The tree and the boosted model start from the same cut.

Now look inside the right box. It has 70 sharks, with an average of 0.363 kg and a squared error of 0.857. The best question there is "length ≤ 54.55 cm?". It sends 64 sharks to the yes side, with an average of 0.338 kg and a squared error of 0.358. It sends the 6 longest sharks to the no side, with an average of 0.626 kg and a squared error of 0.045.

0.8567error of the right box: 70 sharks, average 0.363 kg−0.3581yes side: 64 sharks, average 0.338 kg−0.0454no side: 6 sharks, average 0.626 kg=0.453drop in squared error

The search peels off the few longest and heaviest sharks, because large gaps from one average cost the most squared error. Those 6 sharks are the two highest steps of the depth-3 tree.

Why the average

Why the average? A leaf must give one answer \(c\) to all its sharks. The squared error of that answer is \(\sum_i (y_i - c)^2\). Its slope in \(c\) is \(-2\sum_i (y_i - c)\), which is zero when \(\sum_i y_i = n\,c\). That is the average of the \(y_i\). The error is a bowl in \(c\) (A2), so the zero slope is the lowest point.

The path of Tag 3305, and the highest steps

Tag 3305 answers “yes” to “length ≤ 42.15?”, then “no” to “≤ 34.95?” and “no” to “≤ 39.45?”, and so ends in its step of 21 sharks. The two highest steps (0.55 and 0.70 kg) rest on only 3 sharks per step, from 54.7 to 59.8 cm. Their answers would move if one shark changed.

In practice

In practice, a smallest box of 5 to 20 sharks smooths the staircase and removes steps like those two. A tree answers with averages of training weights, so its answers stay within the range of those weights. For a target that keeps growing, such as the weight of a growing shark, check what happens beyond the training range.

Debug tip. If a regression tree has many steps and the held-out error is much higher than the training error, plot the steps against the held-out points. Steps that follow single noisy sharks show that the smallest box size is too low.

Used in: In A6, small regression trees are added one after another to fit what the earlier trees missed. That is boosting.

In Python

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor

df = pd.read_csv("catch.csv")                  # made-up records
sp = df[df.species == "spadenose"]
tr, he = sp[sp.record_id % 10 >= 3], sp[sp.record_id % 10 < 3]
x, y = tr[["length_cm"]].to_numpy(), tr.weight_kg.to_numpy()
xh, yh = he[["length_cm"]].to_numpy(), he.weight_kg.to_numpy()

def rmse(a, b):
    return float(np.sqrt(np.mean((a - b) ** 2)))

print("average only", round(rmse(y.mean(), y), 4), round(rmse(y.mean(), yh), 4))
for depth in (1, 2, 3, 4, 6):
    tree = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=depth, random_state=0).fit(x, y)
    a, b = rmse(tree.predict(x), y), rmse(tree.predict(xh), yh)
    print(depth, tree.get_n_leaves(), round(a, 4), round(b, 4))

tree = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=3, random_state=0).fit(x, y)
print(tree.predict([[41.0], [60.0], [70.0]]).round(3))
average only 0.1345 0.1582
1 2 0.0812 0.0896
2 4 0.0522 0.0673
3 8 0.036 0.0447
4 16 0.0313 0.0411
6 50 0.0243 0.0491
[0.215 0.7   0.7  ]

The depth-3 row matches the figure: 8 steps, 0.036 kg on the training sharks and 0.045 kg on the held-out sharks. The held-out error is lowest at depth 4 and rises after it, while the training error keeps falling. The last line shows the tree answering 0.215 kg at 41 cm and the same 0.700 kg at 60 and 70 cm.

More questions

Why does the tree's line go flat beyond 60 cm?

No training shark was longer than about 60 cm, so the last box covers all lengths above its threshold and answers with one average.

Exercises

Theory

  1. theory A box has 12 spadenose and 4 other sharks. A question sends 10 spadenose and 1 other shark to the yes side, and the rest to the no side. Find \(G\) before, \(G\) of both sides, the weighted \(G\) after, and the drop.

    Hint

    Write the shares \(p_0\) and \(p_1\) of all three boxes first. The weights are \(n_L/n\) and \(n_R/n\).

  2. theory For two classes show that \(G = 2p(1-p)\), find the value of \(p\) where \(G\) is largest, and give that largest value. Then explain in two sentences why a split can never raise the weighted \(G\).

    Hint

    Expand \(1 - p^2 - (1-p)^2\). For the second part, think about where a weighted average of two points on a downward-bending curve lies.

  3. theory For \(n\) training sharks a computer scores all cut points of one measurement. Compare two methods for scoring all cuts: recounting the classes on both sides from scratch for the cut being tried, and keeping running counts. How many steps does the first need, and how many the second, as functions of \(n\), once the sharks are sorted?

  4. theory Four points lie at the corners of a square: (0, 0) and (1, 1) are class 0, and (0, 1) and (1, 0) are class 1. Show that any first question leaves the weighted \(G\) at 0.5. Then show that a depth-2 tree gives \(G = 0\).

Practice

  1. practice Using best_split from the chapter and the training table, grow the depth-2 tree by hand: find the best split of the whole table, then the best split inside both boxes. Compare your four leaves and thresholds with export_text.

  2. practice Change the label to "hammerhead or not", keep length and depth, and fit trees of depth 1, 2 and 3 with scikit-learn. Compare the held-out accuracy with the lazy answer "not hammerhead". What does this tell you about using accuracy for a rare class (A4)?

    Hint

    Use the same held-out rule: tags ending in 0, 1 or 2. Count how many hammerheads are in the training sharks and the held-out sharks.

  3. practice Divide the length column by 2.54 (inches) and refit the depth-3 classification tree. Compare the predictions with the first tree. Then replace length with (length - 50) ** 2 and refit. Which change alters the tree, and why?

  4. practice Fit regression trees of depth 1 to 8 for the weight of spadenose sharks from length, and print the training and held-out RMSE for these depths. Pick a depth, and compare its held-out RMSE with the straight line from A2.

Think deeper

  1. open SharkCam must flag hammerhead sharks, which are rare in the made-up table (9.5%). Which mistake costs more: calling a hammerhead "other", or calling another shark "hammerhead"? How would you change the tree or its calls, and what would you measure to check?

  2. open The question "depth at most 5.65 m?" works because of how the made-up table was built: the shallow dives are in rock pools and mostly record bamboo sharks. Name two ways such a shortcut could fail when SharkCam is used in a new place. How would you test for it before trusting the tree?

  3. open A tree draws boxes with straight, axis-aligned edges, and logistic regression draws one slanted line. Design an experiment on the catch table that shows which of the two suits a given task better. What would you plot, and what would you compare?

Come back later

Try these after two days, and again after a week. Answer first, then open the box.

A tree's held-out accuracy is 86.0% on 164 sharks. About how far could the true accuracy be from that number, and which toolkit idea tells you? (0.7)

About 2.7 points either way for one standard error, from \(\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}\). The same sampling noise that makes a few coin flips unreliable makes a small held-out set unreliable.

Growing a tree is recursive. What are the base cases, and how is that like the function total(n) in 0.2?

Stop when a box is pure, when it has too few sharks, or when the depth limit is reached. These are the cases answered directly, as total(0) is. The recursive case splits the box and grows a smaller tree in both halves.

The path to box 2 is "length ≤ 50.35 AND depth > 5.65". Which logic operator joins the questions on a path, and which joins the paths that make the same call? (0.4)

AND joins the questions along one path. OR joins the different paths that end in boxes with the same call. A tree is a set of AND rules combined with OR.
